title: First Aid and Emergencies
bigQuestion: What can a young person do to help when someone is hurt or sick?

story.title: Rosa Makes the Call
story.kicker: When her grandfather fell, a ten-year-old girl remembered what to do.
paragraphs: Rosa was doing homework at the kitchen table. Her grandfather was in the next room, reaching for a box on a high shelf. Then she heard a loud thump. She ran in. Grandpa was on the floor. He was awake, but he could not get up, and his arm looked hurt.

Rosa's heart pounded. She wanted to cry. Then she remembered what her teacher had said: take a deep breath first. She breathed in slowly. She told Grandpa, "Stay still. I am getting help." No other grown-up was home.

Rosa picked up the phone and dialed 911. A calm voice asked, "What is your emergency?" Rosa said her grandfather fell and could not get up. She gave her home address, street and number, just the way she had practiced. She answered each question and did not hang up.
The helper on the phone told Rosa to unlock the front door and stay with Grandpa. Soon an ambulance arrived. The paramedics checked Grandpa and took him to the hospital to look at his arm.
Later, Grandpa squeezed Rosa's hand. "You stayed calm," he said. "You knew what to do." Rosa smiled. Knowing her address and practicing the call had made a real difference.
story.think: What did Rosa do first, before she made the call? Why did that help?

lessons.title: Cleaning a Small Cut
lessons.mainIdea: For a small cut, wash it with clean water, cover it with a bandage and tell an adult.
reading: Jada trips on the sidewalk and scrapes her hand. It stings, and there is a little blood. This is a small cut. Knowing a few steps helps her feel calm. Helping someone with a small hurt is called *first aid*.

First, wash the cut gently with clean water. Soap around the cut helps too. This rinses out dirt and germs. Next, press with a clean cloth if it is still bleeding. Then cover it with a *bandage* to keep it clean.
Always tell an adult about a cut. An adult can check it. A cut that is deep, will not stop bleeding, or gets red, puffy and warm later needs a doctor or nurse.

words.d: the first help given to someone who is hurt or sick, before a doctor arrives
a strip or pad that covers a cut to keep it clean

look.title: Jada's Three Steps
look.text: Jada's scraped hand has dirt in it. She goes inside. She rinses it under the faucet. She presses a clean cloth on it. Then she puts on a bandage and shows her mom.
look.prompt: Put Jada's steps in order in your own words. Which step keeps germs out?

check.q: What is the first step for a small cut?
choices: Wash it gently with clean water
check.why: Washing rinses out dirt and germs first.

check.q: Why do we cover a cut with a bandage?
check.why: A bandage keeps the cut clean.

check.q: Which cut needs a doctor or nurse?
choices: A tiny scratch that stopped bleeding
A deep cut that will not stop bleeding
A cut that is healing well
check.why: Deep cuts or cuts that will not stop bleeding need a doctor or nurse.

lessons.title: Helping a Nosebleed
lessons.mainIdea: For a nosebleed, sit up, lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose.
reading: Ben is reading when his nose starts to bleed. Nosebleeds happen often, especially when the air is dry. Most stop on their own with the right care.

Ben sits up and leans a little *forward*. This keeps blood from running down his throat. He *pinches* the soft part of his nose, just below the hard bony part. He breathes through his mouth and keeps pinching for about 10 minutes.

Leaning back is an old habit, but it is not the best idea. Blood can go down the throat and upset the stomach. Ben tells an adult. If a nosebleed does not stop or came from a hard hit, an adult should get medical help.

words.d: toward the front
presses something tightly between the thumb and finger

look.title: Two Ways to Sit
look.text: Picture two kids with nosebleeds. One tips her head way back and looks at the ceiling. The other sits up, leans a little forward and pinches the soft part of his nose.
look.prompt: Which kid is doing it the helpful way? Explain why using the reading.

check.q: Which way should you lean for a nosebleed?
check.why: Leaning forward keeps blood from running down the throat.

check.q: Where should you pinch?
choices: The hard bony top of the nose
The soft part of the nose
check.why: The reading says to pinch the soft part, below the bony part.

check.q: Why is leaning back not a good idea?
choices: Blood can go down the throat.
check.why: Blood can run down the throat and upset the stomach.

lessons.title: Cooling a Burn
lessons.mainIdea: For a small burn, cool it under cool running water and tell an adult; do not use ice or butter.
reading: Mia touches a hot pan by mistake. Her finger turns red and hurts. This is a small *burn*. A burn is an injury from heat, like a stove, hot water or the sun.
The first step is to cool the burn. Hold it under *cool running water* for several minutes, until it feels better. Do not use ice. Ice can hurt the skin more. Do not put butter or oil on it either.
Tell an adult right away. An adult can cover a small burn loosely with a clean bandage. A big burn, a burn on the face, or a burn with blisters needs a doctor or nurse.

words.d: an injury to the skin from heat, fire, hot liquid or the sun
water from a faucet that is cool, not icy, used to cool a burn

look.title: What the Red Cross Teaches
look.text: For a small burn, stop the burning and cool it with cool running water. Do not use ice. Cover it loosely with a clean dressing. Get medical help for large or serious burns.
look.cite: American Red Cross, First Aid/CPR/AED Participant's Manual (burn care guidance)
look.prompt: Which step in the Red Cross advice matches Mia's first step?

check.q: What should Mia do first for her burn?
choices: Cool it under cool running water
check.why: Cool running water is the first step for a small burn.

check.q: Why not use ice on a burn?
choices: Ice can hurt the skin more.
Ice spreads germs to the air.
check.why: The reading says ice can hurt the skin more.

check.q: Which burn needs a doctor or nurse?
choices: A tiny red spot that feels better
A big burn or one with blisters
check.why: Big burns, burns on the face and blistered burns need medical help.

lessons.title: When to Call 911
lessons.mainIdea: Call 911 when someone is in danger right now, like when they cannot breathe, will not wake up or is badly hurt.
reading: In the United States, 911 is the number to call in an *emergency*. An emergency is when someone is in danger right now and needs help fast. The call is free from any phone.
Call 911 if someone will not wake up, cannot breathe, is bleeding a lot, or is badly hurt. Call if you see a fire. If a grown-up is nearby, get them first. If not, you can call.
Do not call 911 as a joke or a test. Helpers must be free for real emergencies. The person who answers is a *dispatcher*. The dispatcher sends police, firefighters or an ambulance.

words.d: a time when someone is in danger and needs help right away
the trained person who answers 911 calls and sends help

look.title: A Very Busy Number
rows: Calls to 911 in the U.S. each year
Calls to 911 in the U.S. each day
Exposure cases handled by poison centers each year
look.cite: National Emergency Number Association (NENA), 9-1-1 statistics; America's Poison Centers, annual reports
look.prompt: Why do you think so many people call 911? Why is it important not to make joke calls?

check.q: Which is an emergency?
choices: A friend will not wake up.
check.why: Someone who will not wake up is in danger and needs help now.

check.q: Who answers a 911 call?
check.why: A trained dispatcher answers and sends help.

check.q: Why should you never call 911 as a joke?
choices: It costs a lot of money.
Helpers must stay free for real emergencies.
check.why: Joke calls take helpers away from people who really need them.

lessons.title: What to Say on the Call
lessons.mainIdea: On a 911 call, say what happened and where you are, answer the questions and do not hang up until told.
reading: Remember Rosa? When she called, she said what happened: Grandpa fell and could not get up. Then she gave her *address*. An address is the street name and number of a home or building.
Knowing your address is a big help. Practice saying it with a grown-up. If you are not home, look for a street sign or a store name. Say your city too.
Answer each question the dispatcher asks. Speak slowly and clearly. Do not hang up until the dispatcher says you can. The dispatcher may give *instructions*, like unlocking the door.

words.d: the street number, street name and city of a place
steps someone tells you to follow

look.title: Practice Script
look.text: Dispatcher: 911, what is your emergency? Caller: My grandpa fell and cannot get up. Dispatcher: What is your address? Caller: 412 Maple Street, Springfield. Dispatcher: Stay on the line with me.
look.prompt: Practice this script with a partner, using your own address with a grown-up's help. What two things did the caller say?

check.q: What two things should you tell the dispatcher first?
choices: What happened and where you are
check.why: The dispatcher needs to know what happened and where to send help.

check.q: What should you do if you are not home and do not know the address?
choices: Look for a street sign or store name
check.why: Street signs and store names help helpers find you.

check.q: When should you hang up?
choices: When the dispatcher says you can
check.why: Stay on the line until the dispatcher tells you it is okay.

lessons.title: Calling Poison Control
lessons.mainIdea: If someone may have swallowed or touched something harmful, an adult can call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.
reading: Little Theo finds a bottle under the sink and takes a sip. His big sister sees. She knows cleaners can be harmful. She gets their dad right away.

Dad calls *Poison Control* at 1-800-222-1222. That number works across the United States, any time of day or night. Experts there tell callers what to do. A *poison* is something that can hurt the body if swallowed, breathed in or touched.
If the person will not wake up or cannot breathe, call 911 instead. To stay safe, never taste things you do not know. Medicines, cleaners and plant sprays should be kept up high or locked away.

words.d: a free helpline, 1-800-222-1222, with experts who say what to do about poisons
something that can hurt the body if swallowed, breathed in or touched

look.title: The Poison Help Line
look.text: The Poison Help line, 1-800-222-1222, connects callers anywhere in the United States to their local poison center. It is free and open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
look.cite: U.S. Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), Poison Help program
look.prompt: Why might it help to put this number on your refrigerator at home?

check.q: What is the Poison Control number?
check.why: Poison Control is 1-800-222-1222.

check.q: What did Theo's sister do first?
check.why: She got an adult right away.

check.q: When should you call 911 instead of Poison Control?
choices: When the person will not wake up or cannot breathe
When you want advice about lunch
check.why: If someone will not wake up or cannot breathe, it is an emergency for 911.

lessons.title: What an Allergy Is
lessons.mainIdea: An allergy is when the immune system reacts strongly to something that is harmless for most people.
reading: Omar cannot eat peanuts. For most people, peanuts are just a snack. But Omar's immune system treats peanuts like a germ. This is called an *allergy*.
Things that cause allergies are called *allergens*. Common ones are peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, bee stings and pollen. A mild reaction may be sneezing or an itchy rash.

A very strong reaction is called *anaphylaxis*. The throat may swell, and breathing can get hard. It needs help right away. Friends can help by respecting food rules and never sharing food without asking.

words.d: when the immune system reacts strongly to something harmless for most people
things that can cause an allergy, like peanuts or pollen
a very strong allergic reaction that can make breathing hard and needs help right away

look.title: Lunch Table Choices
look.text: At lunch, Kai offers Omar a cookie. Omar says, "Does it have nuts? I have a nut allergy." Kai checks the label. It says it may contain peanuts. Kai says, "Let's not risk it," and shares grapes instead.
look.prompt: How did Kai and Omar both help keep Omar safe?

check.q: What is an allergy?
choices: A strong immune reaction to something harmless for most people
check.why: An allergy is the immune system reacting to something usually harmless.

check.q: Which is a common allergen?
check.why: Peanuts are one of the common allergens listed.

check.q: What is anaphylaxis?
choices: A very strong reaction that needs help right away
check.why: Anaphylaxis is a serious reaction that can make breathing hard.

lessons.title: Epinephrine Pens
lessons.mainIdea: An epinephrine pen is medicine for a severe allergic reaction, used by adults, trained helpers or the person it belongs to.
reading: Some people with serious allergies carry an *epinephrine* pen. One well-known brand is the EpiPen. Epinephrine is a medicine that can quickly help with anaphylaxis.

The pen gives a shot, often into the outer thigh. Adults and trained helpers, like school nurses, use it. Some older kids learn to use their own pen with their doctor's help. After it is used, call 911, because the person still needs a doctor.
Your job as a friend is to know the signs and get an adult fast. Know where your friend's pen is kept. Never play with someone's pen. It is real *medicine*.

words.d: a medicine that can quickly help during a very strong allergic reaction
something used to treat or prevent sickness, given the way a doctor says

look.title: A Plan at School
look.text: Omar's school has an allergy plan. His teacher, the school nurse and the lunch staff know it. His epinephrine pen is kept in the nurse's office, and a second one goes on field trips.
look.prompt: Why is it helpful for several adults to know Omar's plan?

check.q: What is an epinephrine pen for?
check.why: Epinephrine helps quickly during anaphylaxis.

check.q: What should happen after an epinephrine pen is used?
check.why: The person still needs a doctor, so call 911.

check.q: What is a friend's main job?
choices: Know the signs and get an adult fast
check.why: Friends help by noticing signs and getting an adult quickly.

lessons.title: Staying Calm Helps
lessons.mainIdea: Taking slow breaths helps you think clearly so you can remember the steps and get help.
reading: In an emergency, your heart may race and your hands may shake. That is normal. Your body is getting ready to act. Rosa felt this too when Grandpa fell.
Slow breathing helps. Breathe in through your nose while you count to four. Breathe out slowly. One or two slow breaths help your brain *focus*. Then you can remember what to do.
Staying *calm* also helps the hurt person. A kind, steady voice helps them feel safe. You can say, "Help is coming. I am here." You do not have to fix everything. Your job is to get help.

words.d: quiet and steady, not rushed or panicked
to pay attention to one thing

look.title: Try Square Breathing
look.text: Breathe in for four counts. Hold for four counts. Breathe out for four counts. Hold for four counts. Picture tracing the four sides of a square as you go.
look.prompt: Try it twice. How does your body feel afterward? When else could this help you?

check.q: Why is it normal for your heart to race in an emergency?
choices: Your body is getting ready to act.
check.why: The reading says a racing heart is the body getting ready to act.

check.q: What helps you focus in an emergency?
check.why: Slow breaths help your brain focus.

check.q: What can you say to help a hurt person feel safe?
check.why: A kind, steady message helps the person feel safe.

lessons.title: A First-Aid Kit
lessons.mainIdea: A first-aid kit holds supplies for small hurts, and knowing where it is helps you act fast.
reading: Mr. Lopez keeps a red box in his classroom. It has a white cross on it. It is a *first-aid kit*. Inside are supplies for small hurts.
A kit often has bandages of different sizes, gauze pads, tape, and wipes for cleaning. It may have gloves, a cold pack and small scissors. Homes, schools and cars can each have one.
Know where the kit is kept at home and at school. Check it with a grown-up to replace used *supplies*. A kit does not replace a doctor. It helps with small things and gets you ready.

words.d: a box of supplies for treating small hurts
things kept ready to be used when needed

look.title: Pack a Kit
look.text: Imagine you are packing a kit for a family trip. On the table are bandages, gauze, tape, a toy car, clean wipes, gloves, a candy bar and a cold pack.
look.prompt: Which items belong in the first-aid kit? Which do not, and why?

check.q: What is a first-aid kit for?
check.why: A first-aid kit holds supplies for small hurts.

check.q: Which item is often in a first-aid kit?
check.why: Bandages are a common first-aid supply.

check.q: Why check the kit with a grown-up?
choices: To take things out for fun
check.why: Checking lets you replace used supplies so the kit is ready.

lessons.title: Helping a Friend Get an Adult
lessons.mainIdea: When a friend is hurt, one of the best ways to help is to get a trusted adult quickly.
reading: At recess, Lily falls off the monkey bars. She is crying and holding her wrist. Her friend Noah wants to help. He tells her, "Stay here. I will get the recess teacher."
Getting a *trusted adult* is often the most important step. A trusted adult is a grown-up you know can help, like a teacher, coach, nurse or parent. Noah does not try to move Lily or fix her arm.
If two friends are there, one can stay while the other runs for help. Tell the adult what happened and where. Being a good *helper* means doing your part and letting trained people do theirs.

words.d: a grown-up you know and can count on for help
someone who does their part to help another person

look.title: Who Can Help?
look.text: Think about places you go each week: school, the park, a friend's house, a store. At each place, there is a grown-up who could help if someone got hurt.
look.prompt: Name a trusted adult for each place. What would you tell them?

check.q: What did Noah do to help Lily?
choices: Went to get the recess teacher
check.why: Noah went to get a trusted adult.

check.q: Who is a trusted adult?
choices: A grown-up you know can help
check.why: A trusted adult is a grown-up you know and can count on.

check.q: If two friends are there, what can they do?
choices: One stays and one runs for help
Both try to fix the injury
check.why: One friend can stay while the other gets help.

review.q: What is the first step for a small cut?

choices: Lean forward and pinch the soft part
review.why: Leaning forward and pinching the soft part is the helpful way.

review.q: What should you put on a small burn first?
review.why: Cool running water is the first step; ice and butter are not.

review.q: What number do you call in a U.S. emergency?
review.why: 911 is the emergency number in the United States.

review.q: Who usually uses an epinephrine pen?
choices: Adults, trained helpers or the person it belongs to
review.why: Adults, trained helpers and some trained older kids use it.

review.q: What helped Rosa think clearly when Grandpa fell?
review.why: Rosa took a deep breath first, which helped her remember what to do.

review.q: How is a first-aid kit different from a doctor?
choices: A kit can fix any injury.
A kit is only for pets.
A kit helps with small hurts; a doctor treats serious ones.
review.why: The kit is for small things; serious injuries need a doctor.
